label: General MIDI standard drum kit, close mics, dry
_takes: A kit fitted one hit at a time has no measurement of what happens between hits, and that is where a drum part lives: the hi-hats share a GM exclusive class, so striking one chokes the others, and the single-hit probe strikes one note every two seconds and has never fired it. The phrase set is what the ear checks that against.
audition_title: libsonare drum kit vs the sampled reference
_channel: Channel 10 (9 zero-based) is what makes a note number select an instrument instead of a pitch, on the reference as much as in libsonare. A drum sampler that answers on any channel will still record correctly here; a GM-conformant reference will record a piano if this is left off, and the corpus would look like a successful capture of the wrong instrument.
_dry: Close mics with the plugin's room and bus sections off. A kit is the one percussion case where dry is both achievable and wanted: the ambience is a mix decision rather than part of the instrument, and libsonare's own send weighting is fitted separately. If the reference cannot be dried - some kits bake the overheads into every sample - clear `dry` and let the room correction handle it, the same way the organ capture does. Here it was achieved: `calibrate` measures RT60 0.00 s, against 3.14 s on the organ capture, so the switch reached what it advertised.
_calibration: From `capture.py calibrate`: the reference renders identically in real time and faster than it, and the measured settle minimum is 250 ms. `realtime` is on anyway, and the reason is a measurement rather than caution. Rendering this grid with it off failed 63 of 282 notes - the sampler returned digital silence and the retry found it five times running - and the failures were not the exotic notes but the snare, the closed hi-hat and the ride. So `calibrate` measuring real time as optional says only that one note on an otherwise idle machine did not need it; a 282-note grid streaming from disk, on a machine doing anything else at the same time, does. Read that recipe line as the floor it is.
_stimulus: 50 ms, because on a drum channel the note-off carries no information: a kit's percussion is voiced as a one-shot and renders identically at any gate. Measured rather than assumed, on the three notes that would show a choke first - open hi-hat, ride and crash, rendered at 50, 250 and 1000 ms - and the RMS agrees to inside 0.1 dB in every window out to two seconds. Worth measuring because the failure is silent: a kit that did choke would fill the corpus with short cymbals and nothing downstream would report anything but a successful capture. The remaining exceptions are the notes a kit voices as held instruments - typically the whistles and the record scratches - whose length is whatever the gate was on the reference side and a constant on the model side. Fitting one of those means re-capturing it at a longer gate, not reading its envelope from this grid.
_tail_by_note: The cymbals need a longer recording than the rest of the kit, and measuring the difference is what says so. At a 2s tail every cymbal's `decay_ms` in reference/drums.json - the time to fall 20 dB - sat between 1170 and 1760 ms against an analysis ceiling of 1800, and five rows were flagged `decay_capped`: those numbers were the window and not the instrument. Recorded to 8s and analysed to `HIT_LONG_MAX_SEC`, nothing is capped and the numbers move where they had been pinned - ride 1 to 2056 ms, crash 2 to 2007, open triangle from 1220 to 2245 - while every cymbal that had room already reads within a few ms of what it did. A flat 8s tail would triple the whole 282-note grid's render time for the sake of ten notes; naming them costs about six minutes. 49-59 covers every cymbal and the ride bell, and is written as a range rather than as the cymbal list, so 50, 54, 56 and 58 are recorded long as well; that costs a few minutes and is cheaper than a hand-kept list that has to stay in step with GM's numbering. 80-81 is the triangle pair. `metrics.LONG_DECAY_DRUM_NOTES` also names 84, the belltree, and this deliberately does not: that set is a fact about instruments, while this grid is the GM standard kit and stops at 81, so a tail entry for 84 would read as a decision and record nothing. That criterion is the time to fall 20 dB, and it is not the only one the grid has to satisfy. `density` and `prompt` are gated on the recording's own noise floor, which needs the piece to fall 60 dB and then stay there long enough to read one - so a piece can be recorded well past its `decay_ms` and still have no floor. The open hi-hat was: at the kit's 2s its tail ended 17 to 39 dB per band above its own lead-in, plainly still sounding, and both terms were refused for it. 46 is named at 5s for that and reaches a floor 2.1 s in, which takes `shape score` from 31 of 45 note-and-layer pairs to 35. None of that moved a single row of reference/drums.json, because every dimension `profile.py` measures stops at its analysis ceiling well before the new tail begins; the length is bought for the floor-gated terms alone. Ride 1 and ride 2 are still open. They are inside 49-59 and still ringing at the end of the 8s, and extrapolating their late slope they need about 18s to fall 60 dB - which is not a per-note cost, because the analysis plane is sized to the LONGEST slot in the grid and every note is padded to it. Recording those two long makes every spectrogram in the harness 2.5 times the size, so it is a decision about the whole grid rather than about two notes.
_round_robin: A sampled kit commonly alternates between several recordings of the same strike, which makes the reference non-deterministic in a way that reads as measurement noise in every metric. `capture.py calibrate` renders the same note twice and reports whether the two agree; check that before trusting a corpus, because a round robin left on puts a floor under the loss that no knob can go below. This kit has none: re-rendering 120 slots of the grid reproduced every good one bit for bit, and a loss that stops falling has stopped for a reason worth finding. What that same re-render did find is a different thing entirely, and calibrate's one note could never have shown it - see `_late_renders`.
_late_renders: A render can come back loud, plausible, and not the note. Re-rendering 120 slots and correlating against the originals, 39 of them returned a completely different signal - correlation 0.000, 4 to 25 dB LOUDER than the real note, beginning 150 to 843 ms into the file after a stretch of digital silence, where every correct render begins at exactly the 100 ms preroll. Whole instruments were affected: all six velocities of the closed hi-hat and of the mute triangle, whose peak levels then read -7.99, -8.03, -8.04, -0.57, -0.79, -0.32 dBFS against a clean ramp that ascends smoothly. Being loud is why nothing caught it - the capture's retry asks whether the samples arrived, and these arrived, late and wrong. `capture.py` now also asks WHEN, retries a render whose audio starts more than `ONSET_SLACK_MS` past the preroll, and records `onset_ms` per slot so the manifest can be audited. Any measurement taken from this kit before that guard existed is suspect, and the whole grid was recaptured under it.
_timbres: One kit, and it is named for what was measured rather than for a product, because the rack publishes no slot names and a label claiming one would be the single unverifiable line in a file whose point is that its contents were measured. `kit-b` answers the whole General MIDI map with a General MIDI layout (a kick low, a bright closed hat, a crash that rings), which the rack's slots reading a 50 Hz kick or a 250 Hz note 42 do not, and its content reaches a median 22.9 kHz. The rack's channel-10 kit is not a reference for any dimension: over 141 of its note/velocity files nothing reaches above 12.2 kHz (-60 dB edges at a median 9.5 kHz) and its hi-hats centre at 2.1-2.5 kHz against the module's 9.5-11.4 kHz. It comes from the same plugin, rack and session as `kit-b`, so the limit is that sample set's rather than the capture chain's. One kit has no spread, so the one bound recorded here floors on the harness's fallback table rather than on a disagreement between references.

timbres.label: Second kit: deeper kick and floor tom, brighter closed hat

_notes: The General MIDI standard kit, note 35 to note 81, every instrument in it. A drum fit is per-note - each instrument is its own patch, or shares one with its neighbours - so there is no register to interpolate across and no note that another note stands in for.
_note_map: There is none, because the six tom keys hold the pitch order General MIDI names them in. Median measured fundamentals across the six velocities: note 41 at 80 Hz, 43 at 85, 45 at 93 to 99, 47 at 98, 48 at 106, 50 at 112 - one ascending series, 45 and 47 inside a few hertz of each other. libsonare's own toms key-track over the same order, so each key pairs with its own reference row.
_groups: Which of these notes are one instrument. A kit is not 47 independent objects: six toms are one series of sizes, three hi-hats are one mechanism at three openings, a mute and an open cuica are one drum played two ways, and every per-hit metric in the harness is taken against that hit's own reference row and can say nothing about the relation. `loss._kit_terms` scores it, as the sorted contrasts within each family, so a family is a SET and needs neither an order nor the note map - the toms group correctly whichever key holds which drum. Which relations a family actually holds is measured from the rows rather than declared here, and the rows say all thirteen hold several: median spread across the six velocities, in doublings, runs 1.36 in pitch and 1.14 in decay for the toms, 3.43 in pitch and 3.05 in decay for the hats, 2.05 in level for the cymbals, 2.13 in decay for the congas, and 5.67 in decay for the triangle pair. The one family deliberately left out is the whistle pair, whose every relation sits at or under the floor - 0.31 in pitch and in decay, 0.18 in colour, 0.20 in level - and whose length is the 50 ms gate rather than the instrument, see `_stimulus`. A relation fitted to that fits the capture recipe.
_bandwidth: The capture carries its whole band. `measure_band_edge` finds no ceiling on `kit-b`: the interquartile spread of the band profile across its 282 rows holds between 25 and 34 dB from 4 kHz up to 12.5 kHz, so every band still tells one instrument from another and `band_edge_hz` is null. None of the bands matters to a bound recorded here, since the one dimension this capture gates is a level span, but they are what `agree` and the audition page read. When a capture does carry an edge, both sides of a comparison are measured with it applied - the band profile, the per-octave decay and the centroid's integration range alike - so a model with a real wash is neither charged for it nor allowed to normalise its whole profile against it.
_velocities: Velocity is the only axis a drum note has, so the grid carries both the set a fit is scored on (64, 100, 127) and the set it is validated against (48, 88, 112) from the same capture. Rendering the holdout now is what makes the generalisation check free later; capturing only the fit set makes it impossible.
_dimensions:
A kit gets the percussion dimensions - band tilt, band profile error, per-octave decay, attack, crest, brightness, level, velocity range, ring length, tonality, image and how the colour moves after the strike - because the pitched ones are built on a fundamental (the harmonic ladder, the intonation error, the tone-to-noise ratio) and a drum hit does not have one. Which of the twelve this capture RECORDS A BOUND FROM is a second question, and it is policy's rather than the metric set's. `policy.json`'s `reference_layer` gives a kit the machine on BOTH axes: the behaviour half - `band_decay`, `ring`, `attack`, `crest`, `level` - was always the module's and is recorded against its own captures and excused below, and the colour half joined it because a modern library's kit is a different set of drums in a different layout rather than the same kit recorded better, so following its colour moves which instrument a note reaches. The colour bounds have now moved to `drums_module_hit.json`, which reads 44 of the kit's 47 keys off the module at a 60 ms gate against this grid's 50, so the same part of the hit is read from the source the policy actually aims at; the four are excused below rather than deleted, because this grid still measures them on every row and the readings quoted further down are those measurements. `vel_range` is the one dimension that genuinely stays here and `_vel_range` says why - the module holds one recording per note, so what a harder stroke does is the one thing its recordings cannot answer at all. All twelve are named rather than left empty, and the difference is what the list asserts: empty means 'whatever was measured', so a gate's bounds would be a byproduct of the measurement rather than a claim about what this kit is judged on, and a dimension that quietly stopped being produced would read as one fewer bound and nothing else. Named, the twelve are the denominator, and one that cannot be reached has to be argued in `dimensions_na` instead of vanishing - the same discipline the parity allowlist runs on. Eleven are excused and one is gated; `_dimensions_na` carries both reasons, and they are not the same kind of reason. All twelve are still measured on every row of this grid - what an excuse withholds here is the bound and never the measurement, which is why the readings further down still quote dimensions this capture no longer gates.

The last three exist because the eight before them are all read off a 1/3-octave profile or an envelope, and three qualities are structurally outside both. Every spectral column is a level or a first moment over those bands, so a comb of tones - one per band, each carrying that band's energy - has the same profile as the noise it was built from to a hundredth of a decibel, the same tilt and the same centroid, and nothing in the set could separate a struck bar from a filtered shaker. How long a hit lasts is not in a spectrum at all: `decay_ms` was measured from the first grid and compared by nothing, while `band_decay` - its nearest stand-in - averages only the octaves both sides resolved, so a hit that ends early loses those octaves from its own average instead of being charged for them. And an image is not in a mono mix. `ring` is the time to fall 20 dB in doublings rather than in milliseconds or percent, because the kit spans 24x on it (60 ms of woodblock against 1428 of cymbal) so a median in milliseconds is the cymbals, and percent prices a doubling at +100 and a halving at -50. `tonality` is spectral flatness over the first 300 ms, geometric mean over arithmetic, and it is a different measurement from the pitched set's `tnr_db` rather than the same one renamed: that one masks around a harmonic ladder and there is no ladder here. What it does NOT answer is how NARROW a peak is: a line and a filled quarter-octave carrying the same band energy come back about a decibel apart, so sharpness within a band is still unmeasured and a small `tonality` delta is not evidence about it. It is also the more trustworthy instrument on the metal - `measure_modes` returns twelve peaks for a cymbal and those peaks move by 14 percent of their frequency between velocities of the same instrument, so a mask built from them would be measuring the extractor.
_vel_range: A velocity response is behaviour, so `policy.json` assigns it to the module, and the module cannot hold it: the source declares no velocity layers at all - `velRange` is set on none of its zones - so it holds one recording per note at a velocity it does not state, and all three module captures excuse it for that. It is the one behavioural dimension the machine reference cannot answer at all. So it stays gated here, on this capture's six velocities, which are the only measurement of a kit's dynamics that exists. That is a stand-in rather than a correction of the policy, and it is worth reading as one: what a bound here grades is how a sampled kit's layers span, which is a recording decision as much as it is a property of a drum. It is NOT excused, because an excused dimension is one nothing measures and this one is measured - 47 notes, six velocities each, a span per note.
_dimensions_na: Eleven, and they leave for three unrelated reasons. Five of them - `band_decay`, `ring`, `attack`, `crest` and `level` - are the behaviour axis, which `policy.json`'s `reference_layer` assigns to the module and not to a modern recording, and they are excused here because the module's own captures gate them rather than because nothing measured them. That is the opposite of the usual entry: the measurement exists on all 282 rows and is a valid reading of a sampled kit, and it is refused because it answers for the wrong source. The two sources genuinely disagree, by up to a factor of four and a half on how long a piece rings, so scoring a voice calibrated to one against the other is not a near miss. Five more - `band_tilt`, `band_shape`, `centroid_pct`, `tonality` and `tilt_rise` - are the colour axis, which the same policy now also gives the module; they left this file when `drums_module_hit.json` took them, and they are excused for the behaviour five's reason rather than because nothing measured them. `stereo` is the eleventh, and it is excused because the source a kit is aimed at cannot answer it rather than because this one cannot: the module's three grids are single-channel, so a width there is zero by construction. `kit-b` has an image - `stereo_width` runs 0.008 to 0.999 across it with a median of 0.710 - and whether a sampled kit's panning may stand in for the module the way its velocity layers do for `vel_range` is undecided. Recorded here rather than left out of the dimension list, because the gap is real and belongs in coverage: nothing bounds a kit's image.

dimensions_na.band_decay: behaviour, which `policy.json` assigns to the module for a kit and not to the modern reference. The two sources disagree about it - note 51 falls 20 dB in 220 ms on the module against a median 979 ms here, note 59 in 287 against 1100, note 81 in 382 against 494 - so a bound recorded from this capture holds the voice to a sampled kit's damping while the voice is calibrated to the module's. `drums_module` gates it over a 400 ms window for the pieces that ring past it, and `drums_module_mid` over 150 ms for the ones that stop between
dimensions_na.ring: behaviour, as `band_decay`, and the same two captures gate it: `drums_module` at 400 ms and `drums_module_mid` at 150 ms. `drums_module_hit`'s 60 ms window is the strike rather than the sound after it, so a ring has not begun there and that grid excuses it too
dimensions_na.attack: behaviour, which `policy.json` assigns to the module for a kit. All three module captures gate it, and `drums_module_hit` is the one that reads it across the whole kit - forty-four keys at a single 60 ms window, which is the longest gate every family fills
dimensions_na.crest: behaviour, as `attack`, and gated on the same three module captures. How peaked a hit is belongs to the module's own recording of it rather than to a modern kit's close-mic and bus decisions
dimensions_na.level: behaviour, and the one that is a relation rather than a per-piece quantity: how far the cymbals sit over the drums can only be read where every member was measured the same way, which is what `drums_module_hit` exists for. `drums_module` and `drums_module_mid` gate it as well, each over its own window
dimensions_na.band_tilt: colour, which `policy.json` now gives the module for a kit on both axes. `drums_module_hit.json` gates it, over 44 of the 47 keys at a 60 ms gate against this grid's 50. Still measured on every row here - what is withheld is the bound and never the measurement, which is why the readings further down still quote it.
dimensions_na.tilt_rise: colour over time, as `band_tilt`: `drums_module_hit.json` gates it, where `policy.json` puts a kit's colour.
dimensions_na.stereo: the module's recordings are single-channel, so the source a kit is aimed at has no image to read. `kit-b` is wide (median 0.710), and whether its panning may stand in for the module's the way its velocity layers do is undecided, so no bound is recorded from it

_identity: Which product this is captured from lives in the untracked sibling `drums.local.json`: the plugin's component triple and each timbre's preset. Everything here is the method. Re-capturing needs the overlay; scoring and fitting read the rendered corpus and need nothing.
